# What Does Cursor Store on Your Machine? A Deep Dive into ~/.cursor/ and state.vscdb

2\.1 GB in ~/.cursor/, another 4.9 GB in Application Support, and a 1.2 GB state.vscdb. Cursor's local data is everywhere: transcripts, SQLite chat stores, global state blobs, checkpoints, and editor history.

Run this right now:

```
du  -sh  ~/.cursor  ~/Library/Application \  Support/Cursor  2> /dev/null
```

On my Mac, that prints:

|Path |Size |
| --- | --- |
|`~/.cursor` |**2\.1 GB** |
|`~/Library/Application Support/Cursor` |**4\.9 GB** |

One important caveat up front: this is a local audit of one heavily used macOS machine, not an official Cursor storage spec.

The exact sizes and counts on your machine will differ. The useful part is the shape of the system.
I expected Cursor to have one obvious “session log” folder, the way Claude Code has `~/.claude/projects/*.jsonl` .

It doesn’t.

What I found instead was a layered system:

* SQLite chat databases in `~/.cursor/chats/`
* transcript JSONL files in `~/.cursor/projects/.../agent-transcripts/`
* a massive global state database at `~/Library/Application Support/Cursor/User/globalStorage/state.vscdb`
* workspace state DBs, local file history, checkpoint diffs, and even separate AI-tracking tables on top of that

If you’re building tooling on top of Cursor session data, this matters. If you’re just curious where your chats went, it matters even more.

* * *

## Where are Cursor sessions actually stored?

On this machine, Cursor session data is spread across **three primary sources** .

### 1\. `~/.cursor/chats/*/*/store.db`

This is the cleanest “real chat database” layer.

I found **171** local `store.db` files under `~/.

...

That is a very different kind of local artifact from a replay log, so I would treat it as a secondary storage layer, not “where the chats are.”

* * *

## Does Cursor auto-delete old sessions?

I could not find evidence of a fixed local TTL like Claude Code’s default 30-day cleanup behavior.

On this machine:

* `store.db` files older than 30 days: **61**
* local history entries go back to **2025-02-06**
* workspace state DBs also persist far beyond 30 days

That does **not** prove Cursor never cleans anything up. But it does strongly suggest there is no simple “all sessions expire after 30 days” rule visible in local storage.

The public docs I found are much stronger on privacy, checkpoints, usage, and cloud sharing than on local retention policy.

* * *

## What about workspace state?

There are also **97** workspace DBs here:

```
~/Library/Application Support/Cursor/User/workspaceStorage/*/state.vscdb
```

The newest one on my machine contains keys like:

* `composer.

...

* transcript files
* chat databases
* global state blobs
* request-level message blobs
* workspace state
* prompt history
* checkpoint diffs
* local editor history
* AI attribution data

all at once.

* * *

## So what is Cursor’s true equivalent of `~/.claude/` ?

Not one folder.

If I had to answer in one sentence:

**Cursor’s equivalent is a storage system, not a transcript directory.**

If I had to answer in two sentences:

**Cursor appears to have at least two replay stacks locally, plus a separate request/provenance layer.**  
**That is the real reason local reverse-engineering and replay tooling for Cursor are harder than for Claude Code.**

The closest “core set” is:

```
~/.cursor/chats/ ~/.cursor/projects/ ~/Library/Application Support/Cursor/User/globalStorage/state.vscdb
```

plus the supporting layers:

```
~/Library/Application Support/Cursor/User/workspaceStorage/ ~/Library/Application Support/Cursor/User/History/ ~/Library/Application Support/Cursor/User/globalStorage/anysphere.cursor-commits/checkpoints/ ~/.cursor/prompt_history.json ~/.cursor/ai-tracking/ai-code-tracking.db
```

That is the map I wish I had before I started reverse-engineering Cursor session replay.

* * *

## How can you inspect your own Cursor data?

Start with:

```
du  -sh  ~/.cursor  ~/Library/Application \  Support/Cursor  2> /dev/null find  ~/.cursor/chats  -name  store.db  2> /dev/null  |  wc  -l find  ~/.cursor/projects  -name  '*.jsonl'  -path  '*/agent-transcripts/*'  2> /dev/null  |  wc  -l find  ~/.cursor/projects  -name  '*.txt'  -path  '*/agent-tools/*'  2> /dev/null  |  wc  -l
```

If you want the interactive version instead of grepping databases:

```
npx  vibe-replay
```
It already knows how to merge Cursor’s JSONL, SQLite, and global-state layers into a replayable session view, and newer builds can also surface some Cursor-specific sidecars such as request-context breadcrumbs and checkpoint-side metadata when those local artifacts exist.

Cursor stores a lot more locally than its UI reveals.

That is the headline.

The deeper point is that Cursor’s local footprint is not one transcript directory you can casually inspect. It is a stack of overlapping systems for replay, recovery, request context, and attribution.

Once you look at it that way, the scattered files start to make sense.

results.title: Cursor Alternatives in 2026
excerpts: For a lot of devs, the combo is effectively “VS Code + Claude Code” rather than a separate AI IDE. Claude Code excels at what you might call “agentic Git automation.” You can tell it: “Clone the ⁠analytics repo, find how the ⁠User event is defined, and update the tracking schema in this current repo to match it.” It will ⁠cd around, ⁠grep for answers, edit files, run tests, and even stage the commit. You just watch the stdout log (or, in the extension, review its plan and diffs). Where Cursor feels like “VS Code with a built‑in agent,” Claude Code feels more like “an autonomous teammate that happens to live in your terminal and IDE.” Cursor keeps you in a more traditional editor model (files, tabs, and inline suggestions), while Claude Code is optimized for high‑level tasks that touch many files, branches, and repos.

This brilliant tool was created by developer John Damask. A quick look at his GitHub shows he&;s actively building tools in this space, including Cursor Journal, a project that leverages this very server to create development logs from chat history. This tells me the tool was born from a real-world need—a developer solving their own problem, which is often the source of the most practical and effective software. An AI assistant using the Cursor DB Explorer to explain the structure of Cursor&;s local database. Source: jbdamask/cursor-db-mcp How Does It Work? The mechanism is both clever and straightforward. The server script, when run, automatically scans your local Cursor installation directory (which varies by OS) to find the project database files, typically named state.vscdb. It then exposes these databases through the MCP standard, making them visible and queryable to any connected MCP client, like your Cursor agent. This means the data never leaves your machine.
It&;s a local loop of communication between your AI assistant and your own files, which is a huge plus for privacy and security. So, what exactly is inside these databases that the server unlocks? It&;s a mix of your direct interactions and the IDE&;s internal state management. Key Features & Tools: What Can It Actually Do? To truly appreciate the Cursor DB Explorer, we need to look at the specific tools and resources it exposes, following the MCP specification. These are the building blocks your AI assistant will use to answer your questions. The server&;s capabilities, including its tools and resources, are clearly listed within the Cursor MCP settings panel. Source: jbdamask/cursor-db-mcp The Tools (The &;Verbs&;) Tools are functions the AI can execute. This server provides two powerful ones. query\_table: This is the powerhouse of the server. It allows the AI to run SQL-like queries against specific tables within a project&;s database.
For example, the AI can be instructed to &;select all conversations from the `chat\_history` table where the content contains &;React hook&;&;. refresh\_databases: A simple but essential utility tool. It tells the server to re-scan your file system for Cursor database paths. This is useful if you&;ve just created a new project and want the server to recognize it immediately without a restart. The query\_table tool is where the magic really happens. Being able to ask my AI, &;look in the ItemTable for keys related to my cursor-journal project&; is a game-changer for debugging and understanding the IDE&;s internal state. It turns your chat history into a queryable log. The Resources (The &;Nouns&;) Resources are data endpoints that the AI can access to retrieve information. They are like read-only APIs. cursor://projects: Lists all available Cursor projects that the server has detected.

...

Open your terminal and enter the following commands: git clone https://github.com/jbdamask/cursor-db-mcp.git cd cursor-db-mcp python install.py This simple script takes care of installing the basic MCP server dependencies for you. It&;s incredibly convenient. 2. Configuration in Cursor IDE This is the main use case. You&;re telling Cursor how to find and run your new local MCP server. In Cursor, go to Settings (Cmd+, or Ctrl+,), then navigate to Cursor Settings -> MCP. Click the &;Add new MCP server&; button. A form will appear. Fill it out with the following details: Name: Cursor DB MCP (or any name you prefer) Type: Command Command: You need the full path to the server script. A common way to structure this is using uv, which the installation script helps set up. The command will look something like this, but you must replace the path with the actual path on your machine: /path/to/your/.
local/bin/uv run --with mcp[cli] mcp run /path/to/your/code/cursor-db-mcp/cursor-db-mcp-server.py A walkthrough of adding the Cursor DB Explorer as a new MCP server within the Cursor IDE settings. Source: jbdamask/cursor-db-mcp 3. Your First Query That&;s it! The server is now integrated. To test it, open a new chat in Cursor and give it a simple prompt: &;Using the Cursor DB MCP, list all my projects.&; If everything is set up correctly, the AI agent should call the tool and return a list of your Cursor projects, confirming the connection is live. You&;ve successfully unlocked your data! A successful query to the server, here asking for keys in the database, shows the tool is working correctly. Source: jbdamask/cursor-db-mcp Competitive Analysis: How Does It Compare? As an engineer or a manager, it&;s not enough to know that a tool works; you need to know where it fits in the broader ecosystem.
When I evaluate an MCP server, I look at a few key dimensions: Specificity (is it for one thing or many?), Scope (local or cloud?), and Setup Complexity. Let&;s see how the Cursor DB Explorer stacks up against other players in the database MCP space. MCP servers can be categorized by their data focus: specialized local data, broad enterprise data, or external SaaS APIs The key takeaway is that the Cursor DB Explorer is not trying to be a universal database tool. Its power lies in its hyper-specialization. vs. General DB Explorers (MindsDB, `wirdes/database-explorer`): Tools like MindsDB are incredibly powerful for federating and querying \*external\* enterprise data sources (PostgreSQL, Snowflake, etc.). They are designed for breadth. The Cursor DB Explorer, in contrast, is all about depth. It&;s designed for one specific application—Cursor—and provides unparalleled access to its internal state. vs.
Other Cursor-Specific Servers (`vltansky/cursor-chat-history`): There are other community servers focused on Cursor, like the Cursor Chat History server. While there&;s overlap, John Damask&;s tool is broader, providing access to project metadata and composer information in addition to chat history, and crucially, it exposes the raw query\_table tool for maximum flexibility. vs. SaaS Aggregators (WayStation): This is an entirely different category. Tools like WayStation are remote MCP servers that act as a bridge to cloud APIs like Notion, Slack, and Jira. They connect your AI to the web. The Cursor DB Explorer connects your AI to your local machine. A visual way to think about this is to plot these servers on a quadrant chart. The Cursor DB Explorer occupies a unique and valuable niche. Real-World Use Cases: From Theory to Practice This is where the rubber meets the road. A tool is only as good as the problems it solves.

# Query traces with MCP

#### Contents

* How it works
* AI Observability tools
* Example prompts
* Install the MCP server

The PostHog MCP server lets your AI coding agent query LLM traces directly from your code editor. Check costs, monitor errors, and analyze model performance – without switching to the PostHog app.

This works in any MCP client – Cursor, Codex, Claude Code, Windsurf, VS Code, and others.

## How it works

With MCP, your coding agent can:

* **Check costs before and after deploys** – "What's my LLM spend today vs yesterday?" to catch cost regressions
* **Monitor error rates** – "Are there any LLM errors in the last hour?" to detect issues early
* **Compare models** – "Compare latency between GPT-4 and Claude for the chat feature" to evaluate model choices
* **Investigate specific traces** – "Show me the most expensive LLM call from today" to find optimization opportunities

## AI Observability tools

The MCP server provides these tools for working with LLM traces:

|Tool |Description |
| --- | --- |
|`get-llm-total-costs-for-project` |Get total LLM costs for the project, broken down by model. Useful for monitoring spend and detecting cost anomalies. |
|`query-run` |Run a custom HogQL query against your LLM trace data. Supports filtering by model, feature, cost, latency, error status, and time range. |

A typical workflow starts with `get-llm-total-costs-for-project` to check overall spend and identify which models are most expensive, then uses `query-run` with a HogQL query to drill into specific traces by feature, time range, or cost threshold.

> **Querying prompts and completions?** The large content fields – `$ai_input` , `$ai_output_choices` , `$ai_input_state` , `$ai_output_state` , and `$ai_tools` – live only on the `posthog.
ai_events` table, not `events` . Query `posthog.ai_events` and anchor on `trace_id` to read them. Metadata like model, cost, token counts, and trace IDs stays on `events` . Rows in `posthog.ai_events` are dropped after the retention period (30 days by default), but rows in `events` have the same retention policy as product analytics events.
> 
> 

## Example prompts

Try these with your MCP-enabled agent:

* `What are my total LLM costs this week, broken down by model?`
* `Find the most expensive LLM calls from the last 24 hours.`
* `Are there any LLM errors today?`
* `Compare token usage between GPT-4 and Claude for the search feature.`
* `How has LLM latency changed over the past 7 days?`
* `Show me traces where a single call cost more than $0.50.`

## Install the MCP server

The recommended way to install is with the AI wizard :

Terminal

PostHog AI

```
`npx @posthog/wizard mcp add`
```

The wizard supports Claude, Cursor, Windsurf, VS Code, and more.
You can also configure it manually .

See the MCP server docs for full setup instructions.
